parts.title: What Lucy Taught Us
parts.subtitle: A scientific finding in east Africa has changed our understanding of how humans have developed
parts.article:
What Lucy Taught Us
 
A scientific finding in east Africa has changed our understanding of how humans have developed
 
(A) On a Sunday morning in late November 1974, a team of scientists were digging in an isolated spot in the Afar region of Ethiopia. Surveying the area, palaeoanthropologist Donald Johanson spotted a small piece of bone. Straight away, he recognised that it came from the elbow of a human ancestor. And there were plenty more. “As I looked up the slopes to my left, I saw bits of the skull, a chunk of jaw, a couple of vertebrae,” says Johanson.
 
(B) It was immediately obvious that the skeleton was a significant find, because the sediments at the site were known to be 3.5 million years old. “I realised this was part of a skeleton that was older than three million years,” says Johanson. It was the most ancient early human ever found. Later it became apparent that it was also the most complete – 40% of the skeleton had been preserved.
 
(C) At the group’s campsite that night, Johanson played a Beatles song called “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds”, and, as the feeling was that the skeleton was female due to its size, someone suggested calling it Lucy. The name stuck and Johanson says, “All of a sudden, she became a person. But the morning after the discovery, the discussion was dominated by questions. How old was Lucy when she died? Did she have children? And might she be our direct ancestor?” Nowadays, we’re starting to get the answers to some of these questions.
 
(D) According to Johanson, Lucy had an incredible combination of primitive and derived features, which had not been seen before. Her skull and jaws were more ape-like than those of other groups of early humans. Her braincase was also very small, no bigger than that of a chimpanzee.
 
(E) For Johanson, it was immediately apparent that Lucy walked upright. That’s because the shape and positioning of her pelvis reflected a fully upright gait. Lucy’s knee and ankle were also preserved and seemed to reflect bipedal walking. Later studies of feet offer even more evidence. As an upright walker, Lucy strengthened the idea that walking was one of the selective pressures driving human evolution forwards. Early humans did not need bigger brains to take defining steps away from apes. Extra brainpower only came over a million years later with the arrival of the species Homo erectus, meaning upright man. Though big brains would clearly be important later, walking remains one of the traits that makes us uniquely human.
 
(F) She may have walked like a human, but Lucy spent at least some of her time up in the trees, as chimpanzees and orangutans still do today. It may be that upright walking evolved in the trees, as a way to walk along branches that would otherwise be too flexible. It’s not clear why Lucy left the safety of the trees. It is thought that savannahs were gradually opening up, so trees were spaced further apart. But hunting for food may have been the real reason for heading to the ground, says Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London. In line with this idea, recent evidence suggests that the diet of early humans was changing at that time.
 
(G) Studies of the remains of food trapped on preserved human teeth indicate that several species, including Lucy’s, were expanding their diet around 3.5 million years ago. Instead of mostly eating fruit from trees, they began to include grasses and possibly meat. This change in diet may have allowed them to range more widely, and to travel around more efficiently in a changing environment. Fossilised crocodile and turtle eggs were found near her skeleton, suggesting that Lucy died while foraging for them in a nearby lake.
 
(H) How did early humans process all these new foods? Later species, like Homo erectus, are known to have used simple stone tools, but no tools have ever been found from this far back. However, in 2010 archaeologists uncovered animal bones with scratches that seem to have been made by stone tools. This suggests that Lucy and her relatives used stone tools to eat meat. There have since been heated debates over whether or not the marks were really made by tools. But if they were, it is not surprising, says Fred Spoor of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.
 
(I) It also seems that Lucy’s childhood was much briefer than ours and that she had to fend for herself from a young age. We know that Lucy was a full-grown adult because she had wisdom teeth and her bones had fused. But unlike modern humans, she seems to have grown to full size very quickly, and the time of death was when she was around 12 years old. In line with that, a recent study of a 3-year-old early human suggested that their brains matured much earlier than ours do.

questions.question: Donald Johanson was uncertain about the nature of the elbow bone he found in Afar.

analyses.content: 文中说 Johanson “立刻”（Straight away）就认出那是人类祖先的肘骨，这与题目中的“不确定”（uncertain）截然相反。
对应句子（第一段）：Straight away, he recognised that it came from the elbow of a human ancestor.

questions.question: Several bones were found by Donald Johanson at the same site in Afar.

analyses.content: 对应句子（第一段）："As I looked up the slopes to my left, I saw bits of the skull, a chunk of jaw, a couple of vertebrae," says Johanson.
文中提到 Johanson 在那个地点看到了一块头骨碎片、一块下颌骨和几节椎骨，说明确实发现了“几块骨头”（Several bones）。

questions.question: The experts realised the importance of the discovery at Afar.

analyses.content: 对应句子（第二段）：It was immediately obvious that the skeleton was a significant find, because the sediments at the site were known to be 3.5 million years old.
文中说大家“立刻显而易见”地意识到这是一项“重大发现”（significant find），因为地层年代非常久远，这与题目中的“意识到重要性”一致。

questions.question: It was the upper part of the skeleton that had suffered the least damage.

analyses.content: 对应句子（第二段）：Later it became apparent that it was also the most complete - 40% of the skeleton had been preserved.
你可能看到了头骨、下颌等上半身部位被提及，就主观推断它们保存得更好，但文中没有这种比较级信息。
文中虽然提到了骨架保存了40%，包括头骨、下颌、骨盆、膝盖等部位，但完全没有对比“上半身”和“下半身”哪个受损更少。

questions.question: The skeleton’s measurements helped Johanson’s team to decide if it was male or female.

analyses.content: 对应句子（第三段）：...as the feeling was that the skeleton was female due to its size, someone suggested calling it Lucy.
文中提到大家感觉骨架是女性是“由于它的体型大小”（due to its size），体型大小属于“测量数据”（measurements）的范畴。

analyses.content: 对应句子（第六段）：It may be that upright walking evolved in the trees, as a way to walk along branches that would otherwise be too flexible.
文中推测直立行走可能是在树上进化出来的，作为一种沿着“树枝”（branches）行走的方式。
对应句子（第六段）：But hunting for food may have been the real reason for heading to the ground, says Chris Stringer...
文中提到寻找食物（hunting for food）可能是促使它们前往“地面”（ground）的真正原因。
对应句子（第七段）：Studies of the remains of food trapped on preserved human teeth indicate that several species... were expanding their diet...
研究人员分析了卡在保存下来的人类“牙齿”（teeth）上的食物残渣，从而推断出饮食的变化。
对应句子（第七段）：Instead of mostly eating fruit from trees, they began to include grasses and possibly meat.
文中说它们开始吃草和肉，而不再是像以前那样主要吃树上的“水果”（fruit）。题目中的 substitute for（替代）对应文中的 Instead of（而不是）。
对应句子（第七段）：Fossilised crocodile and turtle eggs were found near her skeleton, suggesting that Lucy died while foraging for them...
在露西骨架附近发现了鳄鱼和乌龟的“蛋”（eggs）化石，暗示她死时可能正在觅食这些东西。
对应句子（第八段）：However, in 2010 archaeologists uncovered animal bones with scratches that seem to have been made by stone tools.
题目问的是什么东西上有痕迹（marks on them），原文对应的是 animal bones with scratches，所以核心词是 bones。
考古学家发现了一些带有划痕的动物“骨头”（bones），这些划痕似乎是由石器造成的。
对应句子（第九段）：It also seems that Lucy's childhood was much briefer than ours and that she had to fend for herself from a young age.
文中说露西的童年比我们的（ours即现代人）要“短暂得多”（much briefer），反过来说就是现代人的“童年”（childhood）更长。
对应句子（第九段）：In line with that, a recent study of a 3-year-old early human suggested that their brains matured much earlier than ours do.
研究表明早期人类的大脑比我们的成熟得更早（matured much earlier），换句话说，现代人的“大脑”（brains）发育得更晚。
